annotations.text:
Same layout, same real data, three looks. Only the palette and type change — generated from one template so the comparison is honest.

Every colour here passes WCAG AA against its own background. Flip the tweak above any artboard to see a product that passes.

CLINICAL INSTRUMENT

For: matches what the product actually claims — arithmetic you can check. Mono figures line up in columns, hairline rules, sharp corners.

Against: cold. A health app people open in a supermarket may want to feel less like a lab report. The acid lime is unusual enough to divide people.

BOLD EDITORIAL

For: most personality by a distance. The serif headline suits a layout whose hero is a sentence rather than a number — this is the direction that gains most from C.

Against: a serif reads slower at a glance, and glancing is the whole job. Warm brown can read as food-blog rather than nutrition tool.

LIGHT & APPROACHABLE

For: easiest to read one-handed under supermarket lighting, and closest to what shoppers already expect. The safe commercial answer.

Against: least distinctive — it could be any wellness app. Light backgrounds also fight the camera screen either side of it in the flow.

C, refined.

The score is now a ROW, not a hero — readable at a glance, comparable between products, and it doubles as the way into the breakdown. The three little bars are nutrition / additives / processing, so the row hints at the detail behind it.

The verdict moved ABOVE the headline as a small coloured label. Colour registers before you read a word, so you still get the instant yes/no that direction A was built around — without a giant SKIP shouting at you.

Flip the tweak above the artboard to see a product that passes. Every earlier wireframe showed a bad result, which made the whole thing read as a scold.

ONE REAL CONSEQUENCE

The engine writes reasons as list fragments: "11 g sugar — 22% of your daily cap". That reads fine as a bullet and badly as a 31px headline.

Picking C means the scoring engine needs to emit a headline form of its lead reason — a full sentence with the number in it. That's engine work, not styling, and it isn't built yet.
Decided: C. Kept here as the record of what was compared and why — the tradeoffs under each still stand, including the ones against C.

A · VERDICT FIRST

For: you're standing in an aisle deciding yes or no. The word answers that in one glance, before you read anything.

Against: demotes the score to a row, so you lose the at-a-glance "how good is this" people already know from Yuka. A giant SKIP can also read as preachy.

B · SCORE FIRST

For: instantly familiar — anyone who has used Yuka reads it without learning anything. The number is comparable across products, which the other two aren't.

Against: the score answers "is this good", not "should I buy it". The thing you actually came for sits below three bars of data.

C · REASON FIRST — CHOSEN

For: the reason is what changes behaviour. A number is forgettable; "22% of your daily cap" is not. This is the one thing no competitor does.

Against (still true): harder to compare two products on a shelf, and it stakes the whole screen on the engine picking the right lead reason. The score row on the chosen page is the answer to the first half; the second half is still a risk.

These four are less contentious, so they're drawn once rather than three ways.

Two real changes from what's built: onboarding is one question per screen instead of a wall of fields, and "not found" leads with photographing the label rather than apologising.
